description_full: Textron Inc. operates in the aircraft, defense, industrial, and finance businesses worldwide. It operates in six segments: Textron Aviation, Bell, Textron Systems, Industrial, Textron eAviation, and Finance. The Textron Aviation segment manufactures, sells, and services business jets, turboprop and piston engine aircraft, and military trainer and defense aircraft, as well as offers maintenance, inspection, and repair services; commercial parts; and advanced flight training devices. The Bell segment supplies military and commercial helicopters, tiltrotor aircraft, and related spare parts and services. The Textron Systems segment offers unmanned aircraft systems, electronic systems and solutions, advanced marine crafts, piston aircraft engines, live military air-to-air and air-to-ship training, weapons and related components, and armored and specialty vehicles. The Industrial segment offers blow-molded solutions, including conventional plastic fuel tanks and pressurized fuel tanks; plastic tanks for catalytic reduction systems and other fuel system components; lightweight and composite pentatonic battery systems for use in electric vehicles primarily to automobile original equipment manufacturers; and golf cars, off-road utility vehicles, powersports products, light transportation vehicles, aviation ground support equipment, professional turf-maintenance equipment, and turf-care vehicles to golf courses and resorts, government agencies and municipalities, consumers, outdoor enthusiasts, and commercial and industrial users. The Textron eAviation segment manufactures and sells light aircraft and gliders with electric and combustion engines; and provides other research and development initiatives related to sustainable aviation solutions. The Finance segment offers financing services to purchase new and pre-owned aviation aircraft and Bell helicopters. Textron Inc. was founded in 1923 and is headquartered in Providence, Rhode Island.

financial_summary: Textron Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $14.2B market cap on $14.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $929M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.42× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.1×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.70x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+17.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 6% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 18% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.25 vs 5y 0.89), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $128.1M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 57% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 94% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 25% below its DCF fair value of $111, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $89.19 to $142 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 15.0 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 10.1 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 15.2 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 1% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $101 on average, 21% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 9.3%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.49).
It converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.42x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.5% of revenue on R&D and 0.5% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $1.6B (14% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.8% over 3 years, 4.9% over 5 years and 1.0% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 15.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.06 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.3x annual revenue and deferred revenue down 32%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 2.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $22.6M sold).
It returns 5.9% a year to shareholders (5.8% in buybacks and 0.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 5.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 42 consecutive years.
people: With about 34,000 employees, each generates about $435K of revenue, 1.2x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 2.3% a year.
That works out to $27K of free cash flow per employee.
Compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
